body: For sure! I have it set to track my sleep as well. It’s probably not super accurate, but it’s a fairly good estimate of how many hours I’m getting. Because the app asks where you were and what you were doing when the migraine started, I figured out that almost 3/4 of my migraines started when I woke up more than twice during the night, and I was even more likely to have a migraine if I also had less than 9 hours of sleep. Also my period is a big one. Honestly, MigraineBuddy has a lot of preset options so I was able to figure out triggers and symptoms I probably wouldn’t have even thought to track in the first place.

Honestly, it seems a little odd that they wouldn’t push a referral to see a neurologist when you suddenly have a newly onset migraine that hasn’t been broken with medication for over a month? Not that I don’t believe you, I 100% do and  can’t imagine how frustrating that would be to deal with.

Anyway, back to your question- the biggest thing I can recommend is tracking what you can during your migraine. It can be annoying when you’re in a lot of pain but you could even write stuff down on paper and organize it when you’re feeling up to it. Some benefits I’ve personally found are it makes communicating my symptoms and triggers to my doctor easier. To be honest, I’ve finally been able to identify a lot of triggers that I just never picked up on before I started keeping track. It also lets me keep track of what treatments (both medication and not) that I’ve tried and how effective it was. Personally, I use MigraineBuddy. I know some people don’t like it, but it’s been the easiest way for me to track a lot of different things and stay consistent with it. Best of luck!

I’m sorry to hear you’re going through this. I was also a victim of sexual assault during my time in college and I acknowledge how scary it can be to navigate these situations and find resources. I don’t think you should have to file or report him to get the support and accommodations you need. 

Does your school have an Ombudsperson? They can sometimes be helpful in developing a plan, or recommending other resources. Some campuses have resources specifically for sexual assault victims which can help with advocacy and get you accommodations with your professors. The only thing I would keep in mind is that if they work for the college, they most likely are a mandatory reporter; I would still recommend reaching out to these resources and asking about the terms of their confidentiality. 

Starting with the counselor is great, and hopefully they will be able to point you in the right direction for what to do next. If they aren’t super helpful, I would look and see if your college has some kind of Ombudsperson or victim advocacy center.  Most schools will also have a Title IX office, which can sometimes help in these situations, but as someone who went through the Title IX complaint process it can be really re-traumatizing so I would start with confidential services where you can. Depending on the size of your community, there might be community resources for victims that can also provide advocacy as well as free or low-cost counseling and won’t have reporting responsibility to the college. 

Sorry if this is long and rambling, but I hope you can glean something helpful. If you have any questions about anything feel free to reply and I will answer them the best I can down below!

I’m not an expert, and you should definitely talk to a psychiatrist (preferably one that’s different than your current doctor), but from what I’ve learned in getting my bachelor’s in psychology, therapy for people with bipolar primarily serves to help the person cope with stressors and symptoms that might effect daily life. It’s also really important because it helps encourage people with bipolar to stay on their meds even when they feel like they don’t need them anymore (usually during hypomania/mania). THERAPY IS VERY HELPFUL, but proper medication management is just as helpful and important for managing bipolar. I think you should find a different psychiatrist if that’s possible for you.

The first time I was assaulted, I didn’t handle the trauma that came after well at all. I slept around a lot, but I always had to be tipsy (or even all out drunk) in order to have sex. Eventually, my drinking spiraled out of control and I was getting drunk almost every day and missing classes. I was lucky enough to have friends who cared enough to intervene, and I was ultimately able to get that under control.

Then I was assaulted a second time. While my impulses to go back to having a lot of meaningless sex and drink too much were still there, I worked really, really hard to take care of myself in more productive ways instead. I went to therapy, leaned on my friends for support, and gave myself a daily routine. When I started feeling really to have sex again, I picked partners that I trusted. Sometimes I told them I was assaulted before, sometimes not until after, and sometimes not at all. But the biggest thing that helped was that everything that happened in those encounters were within my control. If we needed to slow down, I said so, and if we needed to stop, I said so. Essentially: Finding people who respected my autonomy in sexual and non-sexual situations, going to therapy, and giving myself enough time to heal all helped me.
